## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a22-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Five measures</dt><dd>One number per goal: cost, CO₂, unserved energy, the low-income share of home bills, the gas share.</dd>
<dt>Definitions</dt><dd>Each measure is a choice of unit, boundary and formula; Fair and Secure most of all.</dd>
<dt>Unbeaten plans</dt><dd>No other plan is at least as good on all five goals and better on one: 8 of the 9 plans here.</dd>
<dt>Weights</dt><dd>How much each goal counts; people set them, and different weights pick different plans.</dd>
<dt>Limits</dt><dd>Caps on some goals; the solver finds the cheapest plan that meets them, or reports that none exists.</dd>
<dt>Who decides, who pays</dt><dd>Households and businesses pay through the tariff; a regulator or council approves; people downwind bear harm outside the cost.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Reading a radar honestly</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Scales are choices.</b> Rim (best) and centre (worst): cost $100M and $250M a year; CO₂ 0 and 850 kt; unserved energy 0 and 2,000 MWh; low-income share 20% and 35%; gas share 0% and 100%.</li>
<li><b>Equal weights carry a price.</b> One spoke of cost ($150M) counts as much as one spoke of CO₂ (850 kt): about $176 a tonne, set by the scales, not by anyone's judgement of harm (<a href="12-trade-offs.html">lesson 12</a>: weights carry units).</li>
<li><b>Squeezed spokes.</b> Under a fixed charge per home, every plan's low-income share lies between 31.3% and 34.6%, so Fair scores span only 0.03 to 0.25: a weight on Fair barely moves a pick.</li>
<li><b>Shape, not area.</b> Reordering the spokes changes a polygon's area; compare plans spoke by spoke.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Other ways to measure fairness, security and reliability</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Fairness as burden.</b> <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-burden">Energy burden</span> is the share of income spent on energy. DOE's LEAD tool puts it at about 6% for low-income U.S. households and 2% for others (2018–2022 data). It needs incomes and whole bills, which this town model does not have.</li>
<li><b>Security as diversity.</b> Indices such as Shannon's or the Herfindahl index weigh every source's share, not only the largest; Stirling (2010) adds how different the sources are.</li>
<li><b>Reliability over many years.</b> Loss-of-load expectation counts shortfall hours over many weather years with random plant failures (A5, upcoming).</li>
</ul>
<p>Reviews of energy decisions with several criteria (Wang and co-authors, 2009) find cost, emissions, reliability and social measures in most studies, each defined in many ways.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Five goals as a model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Write each goal as a number to make small, $f_k(x)$ for $k = 1, \dots, 5$ (a [reserve margin]{.lx-term term="reserve-margin"} enters as its negative).

- **Dominance.** Plan $x$ beats plan $y$ when $f_k(x) \le f_k(y)$ for every $k$ and $f_k(x) < f_k(y)$ for at least one. Adding a goal never takes a plan off the unbeaten list.
- **Weighted sum.** Each score is $s_k(x) = (W_k - f_k(x)) / (W_k - B_k)$, clipped to $[0, 1]$, with $B_k$ and $W_k$ the rim and centre of the scale; the pick maximises $\sum_k w_k s_k(x)$. With every $w_k > 0$ the pick is unbeaten; not every unbeaten plan is picked by some weights (lesson 12's dents).
- **Limits** (the [epsilon-constraint]{.lx-term term="epsilon-constraint"} method with three limits). Minimise cost $F(x) + V(x)$, fixed plus running, subject to CO₂ $\le \varepsilon_1$, gas $\le \varepsilon_2 \times$ the electricity used, and a low-income share $\le s$.

The share is a ratio, but its limit is linear. With $a$ the low-income homes' share of the fixed charges and $u = 29.6\%$ their share of use:

$$\frac{a\,F + u\,V}{F + V} \le s \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (a - s)\,F + (u - s)\,V \le 0.$$

| Tariff | $a$ | Low-income share for a plan whose fixed costs are a fraction $\phi$ of its cost |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed charge per home | 34.7% (their share of homes) | $34.7\%\,\phi + 29.6\%\,(1-\phi)$ |
| Income-graduated (half the charge) | 21.0% | $21.0\%\,\phi + 29.6\%\,(1-\phi)$ |
| Per kWh only | 29.6% | 29.6% for every plan |

Mavrotas (2009) shows how to sweep the limits. Upcoming: M6 (carbon in models) and M12 (a city model with screening fairness outputs).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a22-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="winall" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “With five goals, a good plan can usually win on all of them.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Here the cheapest plan (A) emits the most, and the cleanest (I) costs more than twice as much; no plan is best on all five.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="knockout" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Adding a goal can knock a plan off the unbeaten list.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A new goal can only rescue plans: 4 plans beaten on cost and CO₂ alone are unbeaten on all five.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="measured" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A fairness score is measured, just as CO₂ is.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It rests on a tariff. With an income-graduated fixed charge, plans with more building cost (here the cleaner ones) have the lower low-income share, and E, F and G become beaten.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a22">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cd" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Plans C and D differ only by 80 MW of gas peakers, which never ran in 2025. Which measure can tell them apart in C's favour?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">A reserve margin</li><li data-value="b">Unserved energy</li><li data-value="c">CO₂ a year</li><li data-value="d">The gas share</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>A reserve margin: it counts capacity at the peak, 88% for C against 70% for D. The other three see the same year for both.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div id="a22-practice"></div>
```
